Repeated Measures: Mixed Models and GEE for Birth Weight and Knee Osteoarthritis

  1. Using the Georgia babies dataset, fit a model that allows for both
    mom-specific intercepts and trends in birth weight with birth order.
# Load required packages
library(data.table)
library(lme4)
## Loading required package: Matrix
library(readstata13)

# Load the Georgia babies dataset
babies <- read.dta13("data/GAbabies.dta")
setDT(babies)

# Examine data structure
head(babies)

## 4:    39        4     24      15       9    3320    -400        0
## 5:    39        5     25      15      10    2480   -1240        1
## 6:    62        1     17      17       0    2381       0        1
str(babies)

# Fit model with random intercepts and slopes for birth order
fit1 <- lmer(bweight ~ birthord + (birthord | momid), data = babies, REML = FALSE)
## boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')
summary(fit1)

  1. Does this model fit appreciably better than a model that only has mom-specific intercepts? (Hint: consider the change in log likelihood).
# Fit a model with only random intercepts for comparison
fit0 <- lmer(bweight ~ birthord + (1 | momid), data = babies, REML = FALSE)

# Compare the two models using likelihood ratio test
anova(fit0, fit1)
## Data: babies
## Models:
## fit0: bweight ~ birthord + (1 | momid)
## fit1: bweight ~ birthord + (birthord | momid)
##      npar   AIC   BIC  logLik deviance  Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)
## fit0    4 15337 15356 -7664.3    15329                     
## fit1    6 15336 15366 -7662.1    15324 4.4216  2     0.1096
# Extract log likelihood values for both models
logLik(fit0)
## 'log Lik.' -7664.346 (df=4)
logLik(fit1)
## 'log Lik.' -7662.135 (df=6)
# Calculate difference in log likelihood
delta_logLik <- as.numeric(logLik(fit1) - logLik(fit0))
cat("Change in log likelihood:", delta_logLik, "\n")
## Change in log likelihood: 2.210803
# The p-value from the likelihood ratio test
p_val <- anova(fit0, fit1)["fit1", "Pr(>Chisq)"]
cat("p-value from likelihood ratio test:", p_val, "\n")
## p-value from likelihood ratio test: 0.1096126
# Interpretation
if (p_val < 0.05) {
  cat("The model with random slopes fits significantly better than the model with only random intercepts.")
} else {
  cat("There is not sufficient evidence that the model with random slopes fits better.")
}
## There is not sufficient evidence that the model with random slopes fits better.
  1. Compared to either an GEE analysis or the mixed-model analysis with
    only random intercepts, does the model with random trends give a
    different conclusion with respect to the primary question of interest (the
    relationship of birth weight to birth order).
# Load geepack for GEE analysis
library(geepack)

# Fit GEE model for comparison
gee_model <- geeglm(bweight ~ birthord, id = momid, 
                  data = babies, 
                  family = gaussian(), 
                  corstr = "exchangeable")

# Get the primary estimate from each model
birth_order_effect_gee <- summary(gee_model)$coefficients["birthord", "Estimate"]
birth_order_effect_lmer_randint <- summary(fit0)$coefficients["birthord", "Estimate"]
birth_order_effect_lmer_randslope <- summary(fit1)$coefficients["birthord", "Estimate"]

# Also get standard errors
birth_order_se_gee <- summary(gee_model)$coefficients["birthord", "Std.err"]
birth_order_se_lmer_randint <- summary(fit0)$coefficients["birthord", "Std. Error"]
birth_order_se_lmer_randslope <- summary(fit1)$coefficients["birthord", "Std. Error"]

# Create comparison table
effect_comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = c("GEE", "Mixed-model (random intercept)", "Mixed-model (random intercept + slope)"),
  Estimate = c(birth_order_effect_gee, birth_order_effect_lmer_randint, birth_order_effect_lmer_randslope),
  SE = c(birth_order_se_gee, birth_order_se_lmer_randint, birth_order_se_lmer_randslope)
)

# Display the comparison
effect_comparison
##                                    Model Estimate        SE
## 1                                    GEE   46.608  9.996256
## 2         Mixed-model (random intercept)   46.608  9.944792
## 3 Mixed-model (random intercept + slope)   46.608 10.049946
# Calculate percent difference between models
pct_diff_gee_vs_randslope <- 100 * (birth_order_effect_lmer_randslope - birth_order_effect_gee) / birth_order_effect_gee
pct_diff_randint_vs_randslope <- 100 * (birth_order_effect_lmer_randslope - birth_order_effect_lmer_randint) / birth_order_effect_lmer_randint

cat("Percent difference in estimate (Random slope vs. GEE):", round(pct_diff_gee_vs_randslope, 2), "%\n")
## Percent difference in estimate (Random slope vs. GEE): 0 %
cat("Percent difference in estimate (Random slope vs. Random intercept):", round(pct_diff_randint_vs_randslope, 2), "%\n")
## Percent difference in estimate (Random slope vs. Random intercept): 0 %
  1. Provide interpretations of the variances of the random intercepts and of
    the random trends. This may be easiest to do by considering the birth
    weight versus birth order relationship for a woman who is one standard
    deviation above or below normal for the intercept or for the trend.
# Extract the variance components from the model
vc <- VarCorr(fit1)
print(vc)
##  Groups   Name        Std.Dev. Corr 
##  momid    (Intercept) 295.459       
##           birthord     23.693  1.000
##  Residual             443.158
# Extract specific variance components
intercept_var <- as.numeric(attr(vc$momid, "stddev")[1])^2
slope_var <- as.numeric(attr(vc$momid, "stddev")[2])^2
intercept_slope_corr <- attr(vc$momid, "correlation")[1,2]

# Extract the standard deviations (square root of variances)
intercept_sd <- as.numeric(attr(vc$momid, "stddev")[1])
slope_sd <- as.numeric(attr(vc$momid, "stddev")[2])

cat("Variance of random intercepts:", round(intercept_var, 2), "\n")
## Variance of random intercepts: 87296.01
cat("Variance of random slopes:", round(slope_var, 2), "\n")
## Variance of random slopes: 561.34
cat("Standard deviation of random intercepts:", round(intercept_sd, 2), "\n")
## Standard deviation of random intercepts: 295.46
cat("Standard deviation of random slopes:", round(slope_sd, 2), "\n")
## Standard deviation of random slopes: 23.69
cat("Correlation between random intercepts and slopes:", round(intercept_slope_corr, 2), "\n\n")
## Correlation between random intercepts and slopes: 1
# Create a dataset to visualize the effect of random intercepts and slopes
fixed_intercept <- fixef(fit1)[1]
fixed_slope <- fixef(fit1)[2]

# Visualize the birth weight vs. birth order relationship for different mothers
# Get parameters for typical, +1SD, and -1SD moms (both intercept and slope)
birthord_values <- 0:4  # Birth orders 0 through 4

# Reference mother (population average)
ref_mother <- data.table(birthord = birthord_values,
                        pred_bw = fixed_intercept + fixed_slope * birthord_values,
                        type = "Population Average")

# Mother with intercept +1SD, average slope
high_int_mother <- data.table(birthord = birthord_values,
                             pred_bw = (fixed_intercept + intercept_sd) + fixed_slope * birthord_values,
                             type = "Mom +1SD Intercept")

# Mother with intercept -1SD, average slope
low_int_mother <- data.table(birthord = birthord_values,
                            pred_bw = (fixed_intercept - intercept_sd) + fixed_slope * birthord_values,
                            type = "Mom -1SD Intercept")

# Mother with average intercept, slope +1SD
high_slope_mother <- data.table(birthord = birthord_values,
                              pred_bw = fixed_intercept + (fixed_slope + slope_sd) * birthord_values,
                              type = "Mom +1SD Slope")

# Mother with average intercept, slope -1SD
low_slope_mother <- data.table(birthord = birthord_values,
                             pred_bw = fixed_intercept + (fixed_slope - slope_sd) * birthord_values,
                             type = "Mom -1SD Slope")

# Combine all scenarios
all_mothers <- rbindlist(list(ref_mother, high_int_mother, low_int_mother, 
                             high_slope_mother, low_slope_mother))

# Plot the relationships
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(all_mothers, aes(x = birthord, y = pred_bw, color = type, linetype = type)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  labs(x = "Birth Order", y = "Predicted Birth Weight (g)", 
       title = "Birth Weight vs. Birth Order by Mother Type",
       color = "Mother Type", linetype = "Mother Type") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:4) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical")
## Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
## ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.
## This warning is displayed once every 8 hours.
## Call `lifecycle::last_lifecycle_warnings()` to see where this warning was
## generated.

# Interpretation
cat("Interpretation of Random Effects Variances:\n\n")
## Interpretation of Random Effects Variances:
cat("1. Random Intercept Variance (sigma^2_int =", round(intercept_var, 2), "):\n")
## 1. Random Intercept Variance (sigma^2_int = 87296.01 ):
cat("   - This represents variability in baseline birth weights between mothers.\n")
##    - This represents variability in baseline birth weights between mothers.
cat("   - A mother 1 SD above average has a baby weighing", round(intercept_sd, 2), "g more at birth order 0.\n")
##    - A mother 1 SD above average has a baby weighing 295.46 g more at birth order 0.
cat("   - 95% of mothers have baseline birth weights within approximately +/- ", round(2*intercept_sd, 2), "g of average.\n\n")
##    - 95% of mothers have baseline birth weights within approximately +/-  590.92 g of average.
cat("2. Random Slope Variance (sigma^2_slope =", round(slope_var, 2), "):\n")
## 2. Random Slope Variance (sigma^2_slope = 561.34 ):
cat("   - This captures how much the effect of birth order varies across mothers.\n")
##    - This captures how much the effect of birth order varies across mothers.
cat("   - A mother 1 SD above average shows an additional", round(slope_sd, 2), "g increment per birth order.\n")
##    - A mother 1 SD above average shows an additional 23.69 g increment per birth order.
cat("   - 95% of mothers have birth order effects within approximately +/- ", round(2*slope_sd, 2), "g of the average effect.\n\n")
##    - 95% of mothers have birth order effects within approximately +/-  47.39 g of the average effect.
cat("3. Correlation between intercepts and slopes (rho =", round(intercept_slope_corr, 2), "):\n")
## 3. Correlation between intercepts and slopes (rho = 1 ):
if (intercept_slope_corr > 0) {
  cat("   - Positive correlation: Mothers with heavier first babies tend to have larger weight increments with subsequent births.\n")
} else if (intercept_slope_corr < 0) {
  cat("   - Negative correlation: Mothers with heavier first babies tend to have smaller weight increments with subsequent births.\n")
} else {
  cat("   - No correlation: Initial baby weight is unrelated to how birth weight changes with birth order.\n")
}
##    - Positive correlation: Mothers with heavier first babies tend to have larger weight increments with subsequent births.
  1. Using the longitudinal OAI_pain dataset from the Osteoarthritis Initiative. The
    relevant variables are sev_pain (which is 1 if severe pain was reported in the
    right knee in at least one activity and 0 otherwise), BMI, visit (0=baseline,
    then yearly), sex (1=male, 2=female), and race (0=other non-white, 1=white,
    2=African American, 3=Asian).
  1. Use a log link to fit a model to assess whether BMI and sex are related
    to the change in pain over time. Provide an interpretation of coefficients
    relevant to the change in pain over time (you do not need to interpret all
    the coefficients in the model).
# Load required packages
library(data.table)
library(geepack)
library(readstata13)

# Load OAI pain dataset
oai_pain <- read.dta13("data/oai_pain.dta")
setDT(oai_pain)

# Check data structure
head(oai_pain)
##         id   bmi visit maxpain    sex      cohort   race sev_pain
##      <int> <num> <num>   <num> <fctr>      <fctr> <fctr>    <num>
## 1: 9000099  23.8     0       1   Male Progression  White        0
## 2: 9000099  24.1     1       0   Male Progression  White        0
## 3: 9000099  23.4     2       0   Male Progression  White        0
## 4: 9000099  23.7     3       2   Male Progression  White        0
## 5: 9000296  29.8     0       0   Male   Incidence  White        0
## 6: 9000296  29.4     1       0   Male   Incidence  White        0
# Filter out any missing values in essential columns
oai_complete <- na.omit(oai_pain, cols = c("sev_pain", "bmi", "sex", "visit", "id"))

# Fit GEE model with log link
log_model <- geeglm(sev_pain ~ visit*bmi + visit*factor(sex), 
                   family = poisson(link = "log"),
                   id = id,
                   data = oai_complete,
                   corstr = "exchangeable")

# Print model summary
summary(log_model)
## 
## Call:
## geeglm(formula = sev_pain ~ visit * bmi + visit * factor(sex), 
##     family = poisson(link = "log"), data = oai_complete, id = id,

## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

## Correlation structure = exchangeable

## Estimated Correlation Parameters:
##       Estimate Std.err
## alpha   0.2993 0.05118
## Number of clusters:   4674  Maximum cluster size: 4
# Get and print exponentiated coefficients for easier interpretation
cat("\nRelative Risks (exponentiated coefficients):\n")
## 
## Relative Risks (exponentiated coefficients):
rr <- exp(coef(log_model))
print(rr)
##             (Intercept)                   visit                     bmi 
##                0.003466                1.007299                1.101037 
##       factor(sex)Female               visit:bmi visit:factor(sex)Female 
##                1.714306                0.997838                1.020918
# Interpret visit:bmi interaction
cat("\nInterpretation:\n")
## 
## Interpretation:
cat("The interaction term visit:bmi has RR =", round(rr["visit:bmi"], 3), ".\n")
## The interaction term visit:bmi has RR = 0.998 .
cat("This means the effect of BMI on severe pain changes by a factor of", 
    round(rr["visit:bmi"], 3), "per visit.\n")
## This means the effect of BMI on severe pain changes by a factor of 0.998 per visit.
# Interpret visit:sex interaction
cat("\nThe interaction term visit:sex has RR =", round(rr["visit:factor(sex)Female"], 3), ".\n")

  1. Using the OAI walking speed dataset. This gives the
    walking speed of OAI participants over a number of visits. Walking speeds
    of less than 1 meter per second are predictive of poor health outcomes,
    including mortality. The slow_walk variable is defined as 1 if the walking
    speed is less than 1 m/s. In this analysis we will be interested whether the
    probability of a slow walking speed increases with age and whether it is the
    same or different by race.
  1. Briefly (one paragraph) discuss the advantages and disadvantages of

Advantages and Disadvantages of GEE vs. Mixed Models for this Analysis

Advantages of GEE Models: 1. Population-averaged interpretation: GEE provides estimates of the average effect across the population, which aligns with our research question about probability of slow walking at the population level. 2. Robustness to misspecification: GEE estimates are consistent even if the correlation structure is misspecified, which is helpful when the exact nature of within-subject correlation is uncertain. 3. Handles missing data: GEE can accommodate missing data that is missing completely at random (MCAR), which is common in longitudinal studies with dropout. 4. Computational efficiency: GEE models are often computationally less demanding than mixed models, especially for large datasets with binary outcomes.

Disadvantages of GEE Models: 1. Cannot estimate subject-specific effects: GEE doesn’t provide information about individual trajectories or variance components, which might be of interest in understanding heterogeneity. 2. Less efficient with MAR data: GEE provides biased estimates when data is Missing At Random (MAR) rather than MCAR, while mixed models can handle MAR data better. 3. Limited inference about random effects: GEE doesn’t allow statements about the distribution of walking speed trajectories across individuals. 4. No likelihood-based methods: GEE doesn’t produce a likelihood, so likelihood-based model comparison methods cannot be used.

  1. Fit a GEE model to address whether the probability of a slow walking
    speed changes with age are the same or different by race.
# Fit a GEE model to assess whether probability of slow walking speed changes with age differently by race

# Handle missing values
walk_complete <- na.omit(walk_data, cols = c("slow_walk", "age", "race", "id"))

# First, ensure race is treated as a factor
walk_complete[, race := as.factor(race)]

# Check levels of race factor 
table(walk_complete$race)
## 
## Other Non-White           White           Black           Asian 
##             394           21003            4369             210
# Fit GEE model with binomial family (for binary outcome) and logit link
gee_model <- geeglm(slow_walk ~ age*race, 
                   family = binomial(link = "logit"),
                   id = id,
                   data = walk_complete,
                   corstr = "exchangeable")

# Display model summary
summary(gee_model)

## Correlation structure = exchangeable 
## Estimated Scale Parameters:
## 
##             Estimate Std.err
## (Intercept)     1.12   0.836
##   Link = identity 
## 
## Estimated Correlation Parameters:
##       Estimate Std.err
## alpha    0.357   0.266
## Number of clusters:   4665  Maximum cluster size: 7
# Get odds ratios
OR <- exp(coef(gee_model))
cat("\nOdds Ratios:\n")
## 
## Odds Ratios:
print(OR)
##   (Intercept)           age     raceWhite     raceBlack     raceAsian 
##      0.000566      1.083504      0.029868      8.062122      0.002704 
## age:raceWhite age:raceBlack age:raceAsian 
##      1.040628      0.981360      1.089595
# Simple interpretation
cat("\nInterpretation:\n")
## 
## Interpretation:
cat("1. Main effect of age: For the reference race group, the odds of slow walking change by a factor of", 
    round(OR["age"], 3), "per year of age.\n")
## 1. Main effect of age: For the reference race group, the odds of slow walking change by a factor of 1.08 per year of age.
cat("2. Race effects: Compared to the reference group, baseline odds of slow walking are:\n")
## 2. Race effects: Compared to the reference group, baseline odds of slow walking are:
for (r in grep("^race", names(OR))[!grepl("age:race", names(OR))]) {
  cat("   - ", names(OR)[r], ": ", round(OR[r], 3), " times\n", sep="")
}
##    - raceWhite: 0.03 times
##    - raceBlack: 8.06 times
##    - raceAsian: 0.003 times
##    - NA: NA times
##    - NA: NA times
cat("3. Age by race interactions: The effect of age differs by race as follows:\n")
## 3. Age by race interactions: The effect of age differs by race as follows:
for (r in grep("age:race", names(OR))) {
  cat("   - ", names(OR)[r], ": ", round(OR[r], 3), " times the age effect of reference group\n", sep="")
}
##    - age:raceWhite: 1.04 times the age effect of reference group
##    - age:raceBlack: 0.981 times the age effect of reference group
##    - age:raceAsian: 1.09 times the age effect of reference group
# Create basic plot of relationships
age_points <- seq(min(walk_complete$age), max(walk_complete$age), length.out = 5)
race_levels <- levels(walk_complete$race)

# Create prediction grid
pred_grid <- expand.grid(age = age_points, race = race_levels)

# Get predicted probabilities on logit scale
pred_grid$logit <- predict(gee_model, newdata = pred_grid, type = "link")

# Convert to probabilities
pred_grid$prob <- exp(pred_grid$logit) / (1 + exp(pred_grid$logit))

# Convert to data.table for plotting
setDT(pred_grid)

# Create basic plot
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(pred_grid, aes(x = age, y = prob, color = race, group = race)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Probability of Slow Walking", 
       title = "Predicted Slow Walking Probability by Age and Race") +
  theme_minimal()

  1. What are the assumptions of the model?

Assumptions of Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) Model

The key assumptions of the GEE approach include:

  • Correct specification of the mean structure (link function):
    • The logit link correctly relates the predictors to the binary outcome.
    • The linear predictor (age*race) adequately captures the relationship with slow walking.
  • Working correlation structure approximation:
    • The chosen ‘exchangeable’ correlation structure reasonably approximates the true within-subject correlation of repeated measurements.
    • Note: Even if misspecified, GEE still provides consistent parameter estimates, though efficiency may be affected.
  • Large sample size:
    • GEE relies on asymptotic properties, requiring a sufficient number of clusters (subjects).
    • The sandwich estimator for robust standard errors is valid as the number of independent subjects gets large.
  • Missing data is Missing Completely At Random (MCAR):
    • If data is missing for some visits, the missing pattern is unrelated to observed or unobserved values.
    • Standard GEE can produce biased results if missingness depends on observed or unobserved data.
  • Independence between subjects:
    • Observations from different subjects are independent of each other.
    • No clustering or correlation structures beyond the subject level.
  • Adequate sample size in each subgroup:
    • For the interaction between age and race, sufficient observations across the age spectrum for each racial group.
    • Balance is not strictly required, but extreme imbalance can affect estimation stability.
  1. Provide checks of each of the assumptions.
# Simplified assumption checks for GEE model

# Use walk_complete data from q3b which already has missing values handled

# 1. Check correct specification of mean structure
# Create age groups for categorical analysis
walk_complete[, age_group := cut(age, breaks = 5, labels = FALSE)]

# Fit linear vs. categorical model to check linearity
gee_linear <- geeglm(slow_walk ~ age + race, 
                     family = binomial(link = "logit"),
                     id = id, data = walk_complete,
                     corstr = "exchangeable")

gee_categ <- geeglm(slow_walk ~ factor(age_group) + race, 
                    family = binomial(link = "logit"),
                    id = id, data = walk_complete, 
                    corstr = "exchangeable")

# Compare model fits (crude but effective check)
cat("Mean structure check (linearity of age effect):\n")
## Mean structure check (linearity of age effect):
cat("Linear model QIC:", -2*sum(logLik(gee_linear)) + 2*length(coef(gee_linear)), "\n")
## Linear model QIC: 10
cat("Categorical model QIC:", -2*sum(logLik(gee_categ)) + 2*length(coef(gee_categ)), "\n\n")
## Categorical model QIC: 16
# 2. Check working correlation structure
# Compare exchangeable vs. independence correlation structures
gee_exch <- geeglm(slow_walk ~ age*race, 
                   family = binomial(link = "logit"),
                   id = id, data = walk_complete,
                   corstr = "exchangeable")

gee_indep <- geeglm(slow_walk ~ age*race, 
                    family = binomial(link = "logit"),
                    id = id, data = walk_complete,
                    corstr = "independence")

# Compute simple QIC
cat("Working correlation structure check:\n")
## Working correlation structure check:
cat("Exchangeable QIC:", QIC(gee_exch)["QIC"], "\n")
## Exchangeable QIC: 12310
cat("Independence QIC:", QIC(gee_indep)["QIC"], "\n\n")
## Independence QIC: 12266
# 3. Check sample size adequacy
n_subj <- uniqueN(walk_complete$id)
avg_obs <- nrow(walk_complete) / n_subj

cat("Sample size check:\n")
## Sample size check:
cat("Number of subjects:", n_subj, "\n")
## Number of subjects: 4665
cat("Average observations per subject:", round(avg_obs, 2), "\n\n")
## Average observations per subject: 5.57
# 4. Check missing data patterns
# Count observations per subject
obs_per_subj <- walk_complete[, .N, by = id]

cat("Missing data check:\n")
## Missing data check:
cat("Distribution of observations per subject:\n")
## Distribution of observations per subject:
print(table(obs_per_subj$N))
## 
##    1    2    3    4    5    6    7 
##  265  281  249  292  577  658 2343
# Check proportion of complete data
if("visit" %in% names(walk_complete)) {
  max_visits <- max(walk_complete$visit) + 1  # Add 1 if 0-indexed
  complete_subjs <- sum(obs_per_subj$N == max_visits)
  cat("\nSubjects with all possible visits:", 
      complete_subjs, "/", n_subj, 
      "(", round(100*complete_subjs/n_subj, 1), "%)\n\n")
}
